title: Daily routine
objectives: I can describe a typical day from waking up to going to bed.
I can use frequency adverbs such as sempre, geralmente, às vezes and nunca.
I can ask someone about their routine and how they get to work or school.
I can use reflexive verbs and the irregular verbs fazer, ir, sair, ver, dar, ler and pôr in the present.

example.en: I wake up at six thirty.

dialogues.title: Uma manhã corrida
dialogues.context: Ana and her brother Pedro share an apartment in São Paulo. It is a weekday morning and Pedro is still in bed.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Pedro, acorda! São sete horas.
lines.en: Pedro, wake up! It's seven o'clock.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Já? O despertador não toca hoje.
lines.en: Already? The alarm clock isn't ringing today.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Toca, sim. Eu me levanto às seis e meia todo dia.
lines.en: It does ring. I get up at six thirty every day.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Todo dia? Eu me levanto às sete e meia.
lines.en: Every day? I get up at seven thirty.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Depois eu tomo banho, me visto e tomo café da manhã.
lines.en: Then I take a shower, get dressed and have breakfast.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: E eu escovo os dentes e saio correndo.
lines.en: And I brush my teeth and run out the door.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Você não toma café?
lines.en: Don't you have breakfast?

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Às vezes. Hoje eu tomo um café na padaria.
lines.en: Sometimes. Today I'll have a coffee at the bakery.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Então vai! O trabalho começa às nove.
lines.en: Then go! Work starts at nine.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Tá bom. Tchau! A gente se vê à noite.
lines.en: Okay. Bye! See you tonight.

dialogues.title: Como é a sua rotina?
dialogues.context: Mariana and Lucas are coworkers. They talk about their routines during a coffee break.

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: Lucas, a que horas você acorda?
lines.en: Lucas, what time do you wake up?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Eu acordo às cinco e meia. Moro longe.
lines.en: I wake up at five thirty. I live far away.

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: Nossa, cedo! Como você vai para o trabalho?
lines.en: Wow, early! How do you get to work?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Vou de trem e depois de ônibus. É muito tempo.
lines.en: I go by train and then by bus. It takes a lot of time.

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: E você dorme cedo?
lines.en: And do you sleep early?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Sempre! Eu me deito às dez. E você?
lines.en: Always! I go to bed at ten. And you?

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: Eu geralmente durmo tarde. Às vezes eu vejo um filme até meia-noite.
lines.en: I usually sleep late. Sometimes I watch a movie until midnight.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: E de manhã? Você toma café em casa?
lines.en: And in the morning? Do you have coffee at home?

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: Nunca! Eu compro um café aqui no trabalho.
lines.en: Never! I buy a coffee here at work.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Você quer um café agora?
lines.en: Do you want a coffee now?

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: Quero, sim. Obrigada!
lines.en: Yes, I do. Thank you!

dialogues.title: Dividindo as tarefas
dialogues.context: Siblings Bia and Rafael split the household chores on a Saturday morning.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Rafael, hoje é sábado. A gente arruma a casa.
lines.en: Rafael, today is Saturday. We tidy the house.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.pt: Tá bom. Eu lavo a roupa e você lava a louça?
lines.en: Okay. I do the laundry and you wash the dishes?

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Não, eu sempre lavo a louça! Hoje você lava.
lines.en: No, I always wash the dishes! Today you wash them.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.pt: Tá. Então eu lavo a louça e você faz o almoço.
lines.en: Okay. Then I wash the dishes and you make lunch.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Eu faço o almoço e você põe a mesa.
lines.en: I make lunch and you set the table.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.pt: Combinado. Depois eu vejo o jogo na televisão.
lines.en: Deal. Afterwards I watch the game on television.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Só depois! Primeiro você arruma o seu quarto.
lines.en: Only afterwards! First you tidy your room.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.pt: Tudo bem, tudo bem.
lines.en: Fine, fine.

grammar.title: Reflexive verbs: eu me levanto
grammar.explanation:
A reflexive verb describes an action you do to yourself: levantar-se (to get up), vestir-se (to get dressed), deitar-se (to go to bed). The verb comes with a small pronoun that matches the subject: me, te, se, nos. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese the pronoun goes before the verb: eu me levanto, ela se veste. Textbooks and European Portuguese often put it after the verb with a hyphen (levanto-me), but you will almost never hear that in Brazil.

Note that você, ele, ela, a gente, vocês, eles and elas all use se. A gente takes se and a third-person singular verb: a gente se levanta. In negative sentences the pronoun stays right in front of the verb: eu não me levanto cedo.

Many everyday actions that are reflexive in Portuguese are not reflexive in English: eu me chamo (my name is), eu me lembro (I remember). Some verbs that look like they should be reflexive are not: acordar is normally not reflexive (eu acordo), and tomar banho never is.

examples.pt: Eu me levanto às sete.
examples.en: I get up at seven.

examples.pt: Ela se veste rápido.
examples.en: She gets dressed quickly.

examples.pt: A gente se deita tarde no sábado.
examples.en: We go to bed late on Saturday.

examples.pt: Eu não me levanto cedo no domingo.
examples.en: I don't get up early on Sunday.

examples.pt: Vocês se levantam às oito?
examples.en: Do you all get up at eight?

grammar.title: Irregular verbs: fazer, ir, sair, ver, dar, ler, pôr
grammar.explanation:
Several very common verbs do not follow the regular -ar, -er, -ir patterns. Learn them as whole words. Most are irregular only in the eu form and in a few other spots, and the você form is usually short: faz, vai, sai, vê, dá, lê, põe.

The forms for eu, nós and eles are the ones that change most. Ler and ver double the final vowel in the eles form: eles leem, eles veem. In everyday speech a gente takes the same form as você: a gente faz, a gente vai, a gente sai.

Use ir with para to say where you are going: eu vou para o trabalho. Dormir and vestir also have an irregular eu form: eu durmo, eu me visto. Pôr is used for setting the table: eu ponho a mesa.

examples.en: I exercise in the morning.

examples.en: She goes to school by bus.

examples.en: I watch television at night.

examples.en: My parents read the newspaper every day.

examples.pt: Eu ponho a mesa para o jantar.
examples.en: I set the table for dinner.

grammar.title: Frequency adverbs
grammar.explanation:
Frequency adverbs say how often something happens. From most to least often: sempre (always), geralmente (usually), às vezes (sometimes), nunca (never). You can also say todo dia (every day), or use todo with other words: toda manhã, toda noite, todo sábado.

Sempre and geralmente normally sit before the verb: eu sempre tomo café. Às vezes can go at the start or the end of the sentence: às vezes eu almoço fora, or eu almoço fora às vezes. Todo dia usually goes at the end: eu estudo todo dia.

Portuguese allows a double negative. If nunca comes before the verb, do not add não: eu nunca acordo cedo. If nunca comes after the verb, you need não before it: eu não acordo cedo nunca. Both mean the same thing, and the first is more common in speech.

examples.pt: Eu sempre tomo café com leite.
examples.en: I always have coffee with milk.

examples.pt: Geralmente a gente janta às oito.
examples.en: We usually have dinner at eight.

examples.pt: Às vezes eu vou a pé para o trabalho.
examples.en: Sometimes I walk to work.

examples.pt: Ele nunca lava a louça.
examples.en: He never washes the dishes.

examples.pt: Ele não lava a louça nunca.
examples.en: He never washes the dishes.

examples.pt: Eu estudo português todo dia.
examples.en: I study Portuguese every day.

grammar.title: Time expressions and means of transport
grammar.explanation:
Use às before a clock time: às sete, às oito e meia. The exception is one o'clock, which takes à: à uma hora. For parts of the day, say de manhã (in the morning), à tarde (in the afternoon) and à noite (at night or in the evening). Days of the week use no or a plural: no sábado (this one particular Saturday), aos sábados (on Saturdays, as a habit). A range of days is de segunda a sexta. Por volta de means around or about: por volta das sete, around seven.

For how you travel, use de plus the vehicle: de ônibus, de metrô, de trem, de carro. Walking is a pé. To say you go to work, use ir para o trabalho, or ir pro trabalho in casual speech: eu vou pro trabalho de ônibus.

To ask the time of a routine, say a que horas: a que horas você acorda? Use como to ask how: como você vai pro trabalho?

rows: Eu trabalho de segunda a sexta.
Eu saio por volta das oito.

culture.title: Getting around and eating on schedule
culture.text:
In big Brazilian cities such as São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, the commute is a big part of the day. Many people spend one or two hours each way on the ônibus, the metrô or the trem, so they wake up early and leave home before seven. In smaller towns many people go a pé or by bicycle, and a motorcycle is a common way to get around.

Meals follow a steady rhythm. The café da manhã is light: coffee with milk, bread and perhaps cheese. The almoço is the main meal of the day and is usually eaten between noon and two, often at a restaurant that serves food por quilo. Dinner, called jantar or just janta, is lighter and often happens around eight. In the afternoon many Brazilians stop for a cafezinho, a small, strong, sweet coffee, which is offered at nearly every workplace and shop.

When people say goodbye in the evening, you will often hear a gente se vê, meaning see you later. Brazilians generally say a gente in casual speech instead of nós, and that is why the verb stays in the third person.

exercises.prompt: Match the Portuguese with the English

exercises.explanation: Nunca means never. Sempre is always, geralmente is usually and às vezes is sometimes.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Eu me levanto às sete' mean?
choices: I go to bed at seven.
exercises.explanation: Levantar-se means to get up out of bed.
In Brazilian Portuguese você takes se: você se levanta. The pronoun te belongs to tu, which is used in some regions.

exercises.prompt: What does 'de segunda a sexta' mean?
exercises.explanation: De ... a ... gives a range: de segunda a sexta is Monday to Friday.
